title: Supersonic Motion in the Driving Region of M82
summary: The prototypical starburst galaxy M82 is host to an expansive, multiphase outflow whose driving mechanism is not fully understood. Longstanding models suggest that energy and mass injection from supernova into the hottest phase of the galactic wind could drive the cooler phases, but validating these models has been difficult due to the lack of constraints on the hot wind energetics. The high-resolution spectral capabilities of XRISM have generated the tightest constraints to date on the temperatures of the hot wind, as well as the first direct measurement of its velocity dispersion. In this work, we use these new observational constraints to test a model of a supernova-driven free wind. We generate a suite of highly idealized hydrodynamic simulations varying the energy and mass loading of the starburst and construct mock spectra to compare against the XRISM results. We find that the observed velocity dispersion is impossible to replicate using our free-wind model alone, and extra broadening is required to fit the spectrum. We interpret this broadening to be due not to bulk outflow, but rather to smaller scale non-thermal motions in the driving region of the starburst. This implies supersonic motion (Mach 1.71-3.14) of the hot gas in the central region of the galaxy. As supersonic motions are unexpected, it is possible that a significant amount of the energy that should go into heating the gas is instead going towards other sources such as amplifying magnetic fields and driving cosmic rays.

AI.tldr: Using new XRISM observations of M82's hot wind, the authors test supernova-driven wind models and find that the observed velocity dispersion cannot be reproduced by a free-wind model alone, implying additional non-thermal broadening from supersonic motions (Mach 1.71-3.14) in the starburst core, suggesting energy diversion from heating to magnetic field amplification and cosmic ray acceleration.
AI.motivation: To understand the driving mechanism of M82's multiphase outflow by validating longstanding supernova-driven wind models using new observational constraints on the hot wind's temperature and velocity dispersion from XRISM.
AI.method: The authors run highly idealized hydrodynamic simulations of a supernova-driven free wind, varying energy and mass loading parameters, and generate mock X-ray spectra to directly compare against XRISM observations of M82's hot wind.
AI.result: The free-wind model cannot replicate the observed velocity dispersion; extra broadening is required, interpreted as non-thermal motions in the starburst driving region, implying supersonic hot gas motions (Mach 1.71-3.14).
AI.conclusion: The unexpected supersonic motions suggest that a significant fraction of supernova energy is diverted from heating the gas into other channels, such as amplifying magnetic fields and driving cosmic rays.

title: Probing the origins. III. Exoplanet demographics across Galactic birth radii
comment: Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome. Abridged abstract to fit ArXiv's requirements
summary: We quantify radial mixing in exoplanet hosts and explore links between birth environment, orbital evolution, planetary architecture, and Galactic habitability. We constructed a homogeneous catalogue by cross-matching the Encyclopaedia of Exoplanetary Systems with Gaia DR3 astrometry and infrared photometry from 2MASS and AllWISE. Stellar orbits were integrated using Galpy. Stellar birth radii were inferred by combining Galactic chemical enrichment models with the generalised additive model introduced in Paper I. Giant-planet hosts preferentially trace inner-Galaxy birth sites, whereas brown-dwarf hosts span a broader, less localised range of radial displacements. Rocky-only systems show smaller radial excursions and less centrally concentrated birth radii, while rocky+giant systems are intermediate, retaining a stronger link to inner-disc birth environments than rocky-only systems. We also find that outward-migrators host more compact outer detected companions than inward-migrators, with non-migrators in between. This trend remains tentative because of heterogeneous detection biases. Giant-planet hosts retain a strong connection to metal-rich inner-Galaxy birth environments, whereas brown-dwarf hosts span a broader range of radial displacements, and rocky-only systems are less centrally concentrated. The older ages of rocky and rocky+giant hosts, especially among outward migrators, make them useful reference populations for future habitability and technosignature searches. Dynamically heated outer-Galaxy-born hosts show that planet-hosting systems can survive significant Galactic perturbations, although whether their architectures retain causal imprints of this evolution remains uncertain. No clear connection is found between radial displacement and the number of detected planets.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies radial migration of exoplanet host stars using Gaia DR3, 2MASS, and AllWISE data, tracing their birth environments via Galactic chemical enrichment models. Giant-planet hosts originate preferentially in the inner Galaxy, brown-dwarf hosts show broader radial dispersion, and rocky-only systems exhibit smaller excursions. Outward-migrators host more compact outer companions. The findings link stellar birth locations to planetary architectures and Galactic habitability.
AI.motivation: To understand how radial mixing in the Milky Way affects exoplanet host stars, linking their birth environments to planetary system architectures and assessing implications for Galactic habitability.
AI.method: Constructed a homogeneous catalogue by cross-matching the Encyclopaedia of Exoplanetary Systems with Gaia DR3 astrometry, 2MASS, and AllWISE photometry. Stellar orbits integrated with Galpy; birth radii inferred from Galactic chemical enrichment models combined with generalized additive models from Paper I.
AI.result: Giant-planet hosts trace inner-Galaxy birth sites; brown-dwarf hosts show broader radial displacement; rocky-only systems have smaller excursions and less concentrated birth radii. Outward-migrators host more compact outer companions than inward-migrators. Older ages of rocky/rocky+giant hosts (especially outward migrators) make them useful for habitability studies. No clear link between radial displacement and planet multiplicity.
AI.conclusion: Stellar birth environments and subsequent radial migration affect planetary architectures and host star properties relevant to Galactic habitability, though detection biases and uncertain causal links warrant further investigation.

title: Boötes III is a Tidally Disrupting Ultra-Faint Dwarf Galaxy on an Eccentric Polar Orbit
comment: 32 pages, 15 figures, 7 tables. To be submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics. Analysis code and data available at https://github.com/s5collab/boo3
summary: We present updated systemic properties of the ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Boötes III from the Southern Stellar Stream Spectroscopic Survey (S$^5$). We identify 21 high-probability members and measure a velocity dispersion of $σ_{v} = 1.69^{+1.03}_{-0.85}$ km s$^{-1}$, about six times smaller than the previously reported $10.7 \pm 3.5$ km s$^{-1}$, and a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] $= -2.34 \pm 0.11$. The revised dispersion brings Boötes III in line with other tidally disrupting dwarfs such as Antlia II and Crater II. Orbit integrations in a Milky Way (MW) + Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) potential confirm a highly eccentric ($e \approx 0.8$), polar ($i \approx 89.5^\circ$) orbit with a recent pericentric passage $\sim 0.14$ Gyr ago at $r_{\rm peri} \approx 9.5$ kpc. Boötes III is thus likely actively tidally disrupting, as its tidal radius at pericenter, $r_t \approx 164$ pc, is only $\sim 0.35$ of its half-light radius. The unusually low dispersion also implies that Boötes III has either lost most of its dark matter to tides or hosts a cored inner density profile, making it a probe of the nature of dark matter. Simulated tidal streams are broadly consistent with the Styx stellar stream, though the predicted track and kinematics are sensitive to the MW halo mass, LMC mass, and solar velocity. Boötes III overlaps the Typhon stream in integrals-of-motion space but has a much lower mean metallicity, suggesting the two are not the same system but may have had a common group infall origin. Sagittarius-stream contamination prevents a direct tidal-tail detection, so deep spectroscopic follow-up remains essential, both to confirm Styx as a genuine stream and to establish it as Boötes III's tidal tail.

AI.tldr: The ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Boötes III has a newly measured velocity dispersion (1.69 km/s) six times smaller than previously reported, consistent with tidally disrupting dwarfs. It follows a highly eccentric polar orbit and is likely actively disrupting due to tides, having lost most of its dark matter or hosting a cored density profile.
AI.motivation: To update and refine the systemic properties of Boötes III using S⁵ data, as prior measurements had anomalously high velocity dispersion that made the galaxy an outlier among ultra-faint dwarfs.
AI.method: Identification of 21 high-probability members from S⁵ spectroscopy; velocity dispersion and metallicity measurement; orbit integration in MW+LMC potential; comparison with tidal disruption models and known stellar streams (Styx, Typhon).
AI.result: Velocity dispersion σ_v = 1.69⁺¹.⁰³₋₀.₈₅ km/s; mean [Fe/H] = −2.34 ± 0.11; highly eccentric (e≈0.8), polar (i≈89.5°) orbit with recent pericenter at ~9.5 kpc ~0.14 Gyr ago; tidal radius at pericenter (164 pc) is only ~35% of half-light radius.
AI.conclusion: Boötes III is a tidally disrupting ultra-faint dwarf with very low dispersion implying significant dark matter loss or a cored density profile. It overlaps with the Typhon stream in orbital space but differs in metallicity, suggesting common infall origin but not identity. Deep spectroscopic follow-up is needed to confirm the Styx stream as its tidal tail.

title: Physics of Eclipsing Binaries. VI. Hot, compact stars
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJS
summary: Models of eclipsing binaries require the assignment of appropriate emergent intensities to the surface elements of the binary components. For distance-dependent modelling of flux-calibrated light curves, this necessitates an approximation of the absolute normal intensities of both components of the binary, as well as how their brightness varies across the stellar disks (limb darkening). Such surface intensities are often inferred from other physical properties of the synthetic binary (effective temperature, surface gravity, etc.) through the use of model atmospheres, which in turn are generally suited to a particular range of stellar types or parameters. Here, we present the major developments included in the PHOEBE 2.5 release (publicly available from http://phoebe-project.org), which improve the fidelity of model binaries comprising hot, compact stars. These developments include the incorporation model atmospheres produced using the Tubingen Model Atmosphere Package (TMAP) and Montreal/Tremblay codes (complementing the already incorporated PHOENIX and Castelli & Kurucz models, primarily suited to main sequences stars and low-temperature giants). Similarly, PHOEBE v2.5 now allows for blending/extrapolation of model atmospheres, meaning one can continue to make use of model atmospheres in cases when a small number of surface elements have parameters outside the model atmosphere grid. As an added value product, we also present tables of limb-darkening coefficients derived from the newly incorporated model atmospheres, such that they can be used as inputs in other binary modelling codes.

AI.tldr: PHOEBE 2.5 introduces model atmospheres for hot, compact stars (TMAP, Montreal/Tremblay) alongside existing PHOENIX and Castelli & Kurucz models, enables blending/extrapolation of model atmospheres, and provides limb-darkening coefficient tables derived from the new models.
AI.motivation: Distance-dependent modelling of flux-calibrated light curves of eclipsing binaries requires accurate surface intensities (absolute normal intensities and limb darkening), but existing model atmospheres in PHOEBE were primarily suited to main sequence stars and low-temperature giants, lacking fidelity for hot, compact stars.
AI.method: Incorporated TMAP and Montreal/Tremblay model atmospheres for hot, compact stars; implemented blending/extrapolation of model atmospheres to handle surface elements with parameters outside the grid; derived limb-darkening coefficients from the new models.
AI.result: PHOEBE 2.5 now supports modelling of binaries comprising hot, compact stars with improved surface intensity fidelity, and provides limb-darkening coefficient tables for use in other binary modelling codes.
AI.conclusion: The developments in PHOEBE 2.5 extend the astrophysical range of binary modelling to hot, compact objects, with flexible atmosphere handling and reusable outputs for the community.

title: Scaling Relations for Binary Black Hole Merger Times from Cosmological Initial Conditions
summary: Recent evidence from Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) for a nanohertz gravitational wave background is broadly consistent with theoretical expectations from a population of massive black hole binaries (MBHBs), although the inferred amplitude appears somewhat higher than predicted by standard models. Interpreting these observations requires a robust understanding of the merger timescales of MBHBs, and of their connection to host galaxy properties. In this work, we investigate the evolution of MBHBs selected from cosmological galaxy mergers in the IllustrisTNG simulation. We re-simulate these systems at high resolution using the N-body code Griffin to accurately resolve the dynamical friction and stellar hardening phases, and follow their evolution to coalescence with a semi-analytical model. We find that cosmological galaxy encounters and the resulting MBHBs are typically highly eccentric. We characterise the distribution of binary eccentricities at formation and at entry into the PTA band, and quantify the corresponding residence times. We identify the key parameters governing the duration of the different stages of MBHB evolution, and derive scaling relations linking galaxy and orbital properties to dynamical friction, hardening, and total coalescence times. These relations provide a framework for subgrid prescriptions in cosmological simulations. Applying these scaling relations to the full IllustrisTNG merger population, we infer the probability distributions of galaxy merger and black hole coalescence times. We find that galaxy mergers typically complete within $\sim 0.7$ Gyr, while the total black hole coalescence time is $\sim 1.0$ Gyr. These short timescales imply efficient binary evolution, consistent with current PTA constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the IllustrisTNG simulation and high-resolution N-body re-simulations with the Griffin code, combined with semi-analytical modeling, to study the evolution of massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) from cosmological galaxy mergers. The authors find that MBHBs are typically highly eccentric, quantify eccentricity distributions and residence times, and derive scaling relations linking galaxy properties to merger timescales. Galaxy mergers complete within ~0.7 Gyr and total black hole coalescence within ~1.0 Gyr, implying efficient binary evolution consistent with PTA constraints.
AI.motivation: PTA observations suggest a nanohertz gravitational wave background potentially from MBHBs, but the inferred amplitude is higher than standard models predict. Understanding MBHB merger timescales and their connection to host galaxy properties is essential for interpreting these observations.
AI.method: Select MBHBs from cosmological galaxy mergers in the IllustrisTNG simulation, re-simulate at high resolution with the N-body code Griffin to resolve dynamical friction and stellar hardening, and follow evolution to coalescence using a semi-analytical model.
AI.result: MBHBs are highly eccentric at formation and when entering the PTA band. Galaxy mergers complete in ~0.7 Gyr and total black hole coalescence in ~1.0 Gyr. Scaling relations linking galaxy properties to dynamical friction, hardening, and total coalescence times are derived.
AI.conclusion: The short coalescence timescales imply efficient binary evolution consistent with current PTA constraints. The derived scaling relations provide a framework for subgrid prescriptions in cosmological simulations.

title: Node-locked phase of annual modulations from the gravitational chiral anomaly in the solar Kerr field
summary: The Chern-Pontryagin density of the Sun's Kerr field, ${}^*RR\simeq 288\,G^{2}M_{\odot}^{2}a_{\odot}\cosθ/c^{4}r^{7}$, provides an annually sign-changing parity-odd curvature invariant sampled by a detector in the Solar System and sources the gravitational chiral anomaly $\nabla_μj^μ_{5}={}^*RR/384π^{2}$. Sampled along the Earth's orbit it is odd about the solar equatorial plane, so the accumulated chirality is extremal at the plane crossings. Any observable coupled to this reservoir therefore modulates annually with a phase fixed entirely by ephemerides: the cosine-fit phase is $t^{*}=158.7$ d (June 7-8) for a rate-suppressing coupling or $t^{*}=341.4$ d (December 7-8) for a rate-enhancing one, with a calculable secular drift of $+0.014$ d yr$^{-1}$, strict energy independence, a phase-locked semiannual harmonic of $3.75\%$, and no synodic (27 d) or solar-cycle (11 yr) components. The sign and magnitude of the coupling are not predicted; the phase is. A single-amplitude fit to the DAMA/LIBRA-phase2 residuals selects the suppressing branch and describes the observed modulation as well as the standard-halo dark-matter cosine ($Δχ^{2}=1.8$). The most precise published phase, from the full 3.40 t yr exposure, $t^{*}=153.5\pm3.8$ d, lies $0.3σ$ from the halo value and $1.4σ$ from the node-locked one: the $6.2$-day separation between the hypotheses is below the current resolution. Unlike the halo phase, the node-locked phase admits no astrophysical adjustment, so phase metrology at the two-day level, and a test of its energy independence, discriminates between the two hypotheses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that the Sun's Kerr field generates a Chern-Pontryagin density that varies annually, creating a gravitational chiral anomaly reservoir with a precisely predictable phase. This phase matches DAMA/LIBRA modulation data better than the standard dark-matter halo hypothesis, offering a testable alternative.
AI.motivation: To explain the annually modulating signal observed in dark matter direct detection experiments (specifically DAMA/LIBRA) using a purely gravitational phenomenon rooted in the Sun's rotation (Kerr metric) rather than dark matter particle interactions.
AI.method: The authors compute the Chern-Pontryagin density (parity-odd curvature invariant *RR) from the Sun's Kerr field, derive its annual modulation along Earth's orbit, and calculate the precise phase of the accumulated chirality. They fit this phase template to DAMA/LIBRA-phase2 residuals and compare with the standard halo dark-matter cosine model.
AI.result: The node-locked phase predicts a cosine-fit phase of either 158.7 d (June 7-8, rate-suppressing) or 341.4 d (December 7-8, rate-enhancing). The DAMA/LIBRA data selects the suppressing branch. The most precise published phase (153.5±3.8 d) is 0.3σ from the halo value and 1.4σ from the node-locked one, with a 6.2-day separation below current resolution.
AI.conclusion: The gravitational chiral anomaly provides an alternative, testable explanation for DAMA/LIBRA's annual modulation. Unlike dark matter halo models, the node-locked phase is fixed by ephemerides with no adjustable astrophysical parameters. Phase metrology at the two-day level and tests of energy independence can discriminate between the two hypotheses.

title: The DESI View of the Faint Radio Source Population in LoTSS DR2
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The faint radio-source population includes galaxies dominated by both star formation (SF) and active galactic nuclei (AGN), which are two key processes shaping galaxy evolution. To investigate this population, we probabilistically classified 251,413 radio sources from the second data release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS DR2) using spectroscopic data from the first release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1). Our classification method includes: (i) the identification of radio excess relative to SF, (ii) the Baldwin, Philips & Terlevich (BPT) diagram, (iii) a modified Mass Excitation (MEx) diagram, and (iv) the [OIII]5007 equivalent width. These are combined with Monte Carlo methods to estimate the probability that each source is a star-forming galaxy (SFG), a radio-quiet AGN (RQ AGN), or a low- or high-excitation radio galaxy (LERG or HERG), allowing various thresholds to be applied depending on science goals. Considering classifications above a 90 per cent probability threshold, we identify 68,820 SFGs, 32,288 RQ AGN, 35,210 LERGs and 3,085 HERGs, representing the largest radio sample to date with high-confidence spectroscopic classifications. Using this sample, we show with higher statistical power than previous studies that LERGs typically accrete below 1 per cent of the Eddington limit and HERGs above it. We also identify a small subset of high-accreting LERGs whose stacked spectra reveal prominent star-forming features, highlighting difficulties in interpreting their accretion properties. Our results demonstrate the power of large spectroscopic samples to characterise the radio-source population, providing a foundation for studies in the SKA era.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a probabilistic classification of 251,413 radio sources from LoTSS DR2 using DESI DR1 spectroscopy, identifying 68,820 SFGs, 32,288 RQ AGN, 35,210 LERGs, and 3,085 HERGs at ≥90% confidence. It shows LERGs accrete below 1% Eddington limit while HERGs accrete above it, with a subset of high-accreting LERGs showing star-forming features in stacked spectra.
AI.motivation: To understand the faint radio-source population (dominated by both star formation and AGN) and its role in galaxy evolution, requiring a clean probabilistic classification of radio sources into SFGs, RQ AGN, LERGs, and HERGs using large spectroscopic samples.
AI.method: Probabilistic classification combining four diagnostics: (i) radio excess relative to star formation, (ii) BPT diagram, (iii) modified Mass Excitation (MEx) diagram, and (iv) [OIII]5007 equivalent width, integrated with Monte Carlo methods to estimate classification probabilities for each source.
AI.result: At ≥90% probability threshold: 68,820 SFGs, 32,288 RQ AGN, 35,210 LERGs, 3,085 HERGs. LERGs typically accrete below 1% Eddington limit, HERGs above it. A small subset of high-accreting LERGs shows prominent star-forming features in stacked spectra.
AI.conclusion: This is the largest radio sample to date with high-confidence spectroscopic classifications, demonstrating the power of large spectroscopic surveys (DESI + LOFAR) to characterize the radio-source population, providing a foundation for future SKA-era studies.

title: Cluster-Weighted Training of Deep Surrogate Models for Subgrid Turbulent Transport
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables, SABID workshop at 2025 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining
summary: Turbulence in the solar interior and atmosphere plays a crucial role in energy transport, yet modeling its subgrid-scale effects remains a major challenge. This study leverages machine learning (ML) models to predict components of the Reynolds stress tensor using high-resolution StellarBox simulations of the quiet Sun. Previously, we have compared a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) against physics-based baselines to achieve a lower Mean Squared Error (MSE) and better generalization across various heights and depths in the solar atmosphere. To enhance learning, in this work, we investigate cluster-weighted training using K-Means and Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC). By weighing the loss function based on cluster-specific prediction errors, we direct the model's attention to high-error regions. It significantly improves CNN performance, achieving 34% lower MSE and a significantly higher R2 score indicating that integrating deterministic clustering with ML is a promising technique for modeling subgrid turbulence, in particular, and regression in diverse environments, in general.

AI.tldr: This study improves ML-based prediction of Reynolds stress tensor components in solar turbulence by using cluster-weighted training (K-Means and HAC) to focus on high-error regions, achieving 34% lower MSE and higher R² score for CNNs.
AI.motivation: Turbulence in the solar interior and atmosphere is critical for energy transport, but modeling subgrid-scale effects remains a major challenge.
AI.method: Uses ML models (MLP and 3D CNN) with high-resolution StellarBox simulations of the quiet Sun; enhances learning via cluster-weighted training using K-Means and Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC) to weight the loss function based on cluster-specific prediction errors.
AI.result: Cluster-weighted training significantly improves CNN performance: 34% lower MSE and a significantly higher R² score compared to physics-based baselines and standard training.
AI.conclusion: Integrating deterministic clustering with ML is a promising technique for modeling subgrid turbulence and regression in diverse environments.

title: On the detection of Population III galaxies: Emission Line Diagnostics for Hybrid Stellar Populations
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Identifying Population III (Pop III) stars, the first generation of metal-free stars in the early Universe, remains a central challenge in astrophysics. High-ionization emission lines, such as HeII are commonly used as tracers of Pop III signatures. However, realistic galaxies may host hybrid stellar populations, including both Pop III and metal-enriched Population II (Pop II) stars, complicating the interpretation of observed spectra. We aim to investigate how hybrid Pop III/Pop II stellar populations affect emission line diagnostics and assess the detectability of Pop III stars across different galactic environments and redshifts. We select galaxies with varying Pop III-to-total mass ratios from the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations. Using self-consistent photoionisation models, we compute integrated spectra by adopting local physical conditions from the simulations to study the resulting emission line diagnostics. We find that emission line diagnostics are strongly dependent on the relative Pop III contribution. Current diagnostics can identify galaxies dominated totally by Pop III stars but fail for systems where Pop II stars contribute significantly, introducing degeneracies in interpreting observed spectra. Our results highlight the limitations of existing emission line diagnostics in hybrid systems and emphasize the need for additional methods that account for mixed stellar populations to reliably detect Pop III stars during and after the epoch of reionization.

AI.tldr: This study uses IllustrisTNG simulations to model hybrid Pop III/Pop II stellar populations and finds that current HeII-based emission line diagnostics can only identify galaxies dominated entirely by Pop III stars, failing when Pop II stars contribute significantly due to spectral degeneracies.
AI.motivation: Identifying Population III stars is a central challenge in astrophysics, but realistic galaxies may host hybrid stellar populations (Pop III + Pop II), complicating the interpretation of observed spectra.
AI.method: Select galaxies with varying Pop III-to-total mass ratios from IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations; compute integrated spectra using self-consistent photoionisation models based on local physical conditions from simulations.
AI.result: Emission line diagnostics strongly depend on the relative Pop III contribution; current diagnostics work for pure Pop III galaxies but fail for hybrid systems where Pop II stars contribute significantly, introducing degeneracies.
AI.conclusion: Existing emission line diagnostics are limited in hybrid systems; additional methods accounting for mixed stellar populations are needed to reliably detect Pop III stars during and after reionization.

title: A Transport Theory of Turbulent Coronal Heating in General Geometry
summary: Magnetic geometry shapes how turbulence transports and dissipates energy in strongly magnetized plasmas. The solar corona, a maze of open and closed flux tubes with sharp transverse gradients, is a prominent example, yet most wave-turbulence models of coronal heating assume symmetric flux tubes or add geometric effects in ad hoc ways. Here we develop a geometry-complete multiscale transport theory for reduced-magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in an arbitrary background field, retaining squashing (magnetic shear), transverse gradients, curvature, and gravity at the same order as standard expansion-driven reflection, and coupling fast, anisotropic fluctuations to slow background evolution through conservation laws. Applied to the corona, it recovers the standard reflection-driven turbulent cascade in smooth regions such as coronal-hole interiors, but predicts that in structured regions geometry-driven channels can dominate: squashing drives reflection even when parallel Alfvén-speed gradients are weak; curvature and non-radial geometry drive compressive heating channels; and waves catalyze the relaxation of velocity shear into heat. The same dynamics drive cross-field transport of mass, composition, momentum, and heat across open-closed interfaces, at rates rivaling the field-parallel supply from the base. These effects bias heating to low altitudes in structured regions, giving a physical basis for the coronal-hole--boundary corrections used in empirical wind-speed predictors. Additionally, the framework's slow-timescale transport equations could be evolved in time, providing a route to a global, geometry-aware model of a structured wave-driven corona and wind. More broadly, the theory provides an energy-consistent account of turbulence, geometry, and transport effects relevant to various astrophysical and terrestrial settings, from magnetospheres and accretion flows to fusion experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometry-complete multiscale transport theory for reduced-MHD turbulence in arbitrary magnetic fields, showing that in structured regions of the solar corona, geometric effects (squashing, curvature, transverse gradients) can dominate over standard reflection-driven cascades, with implications for coronal heating and cross-field transport.
AI.motivation: Existing wave-turbulence models of coronal heating assume symmetric flux tubes or add geometric effects ad hoc, but the solar corona consists of complex open/closed flux tubes with sharp transverse gradients, requiring a theory that fully incorporates magnetic geometry.
AI.method: A geometry-complete multiscale transport theory for reduced-MHD turbulence in an arbitrary background field, retaining squashing, transverse gradients, curvature, and gravity at the same order as standard expansion-driven reflection, and coupling fast fluctuations to slow background evolution via conservation laws.
AI.result: In smooth regions (e.g., coronal-hole interiors) the standard reflection-driven cascade is recovered. In structured regions, geometry-driven channels dominate: squashing drives reflection without parallel Alfvén-speed gradients; curvature and non-radial geometry drive compressive heating; waves catalyze velocity shear relaxation into heat. Cross-field transport across open-closed interfaces rivals field-parallel supply.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an energy-consistent account of turbulence, geometry, and transport, with applications to coronal heating, wind-speed predictions, and broader astrophysical/terrestrial settings (magnetospheres, accretion flows, fusion experiments).

title: Enhancing Photometric Redshift Estimation for LSST with a Hybrid LSTM-Mixture Density Network
summary: Accurate photometric redshift (photo-$z$) estimation and robust uncertainty quantification are essential for the LSST to achieve its precision cosmology goals. Traditional machine learning algorithms are largely restricted to point estimates, struggling to characterize the multimodal nature of redshift PDFs and the degeneracies within the color-redshift space. To address this, we present and validate the LSTM-MDNz architecture, which integrates sequential feature extraction with flexible probability density modeling to enhance both prediction accuracy and uncertainty calibration across a broad redshift range, thereby meeting the stringent data quality requirements necessitated by next-generation cosmological analysis. The LSTM-MDNz framework treats multi-band photometry as wavelength-ordered sequences, utilizing LSTM networks to capture non-linear evolutionary correlations across the SED. A Mixture Density Network (MDN) is then employed to explicitly model posterior PDFs via Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). Performance is evaluated on the HSC GalaxiesML dataset (which serves as a small-scale proxy for next-generation surveys like LSST) and benchmarked against the BNN architecture established by Jones et al. (2024). The proposed model consistently outperforms the BNN baseline, achieving a $\sim 10\%$ improvement in point-estimation accuracy (specifically across RMSE, MAE, scatter, and $σ_{\text{NMAD}}$) and a $\sim 20\%$ reduction in the rates of both general and catastrophic outliers. A uniform probability integral transform (PIT) distribution confirms well-calibrated probabilistic outputs. Furthermore, the PDF-based confidence metric $z_{\text{conf}}$ enables high-purity catalog construction: excluding just approximately $4\%$ of extremely low-confidence ($z_{\text{conf}} < 0.05$) samples reduces the overall outlier rate by $\sim 48\%$.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LSTM-MDNz, a deep learning architecture combining LSTM networks (for sequential feature extraction from multi-band photometry) with Mixture Density Networks (for probabilistic redshift estimation). It outperforms BNN baselines on the HSC GalaxiesML dataset, achieving ~10% better point-estimation accuracy and ~20% fewer outliers, with well-calibrated uncertainty via PIT analysis.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML methods provide only point estimates and fail to capture multimodal redshift PDFs and color-redshift degeneracies, which is insufficient for LSST's precision cosmology goals.
AI.method: LSTM-MDNz: (1) treats multi-band photometry as wavelength-ordered sequences fed into LSTM networks to capture SED correlations; (2) uses Mixture Density Network (MDN) with Gaussian mixture models to model posterior PDFs explicitly.
AI.result: Outperforms BNN (Jones et al. 2024): ~10% improvement in point estimates (RMSE, MAE, scatter, σ_NMAD); ~20% reduction in general and catastrophic outliers. PIT distribution confirms well-calibrated outputs. Removing ~4% low-confidence (z_conf<0.05) samples reduces outlier rate by ~48%.
AI.conclusion: LSTM-MDNz enhances photo-z accuracy and uncertainty calibration, meeting LSST's data quality requirements. The z_conf metric enables high-purity catalog construction with minimal sample loss.

title: RedDots: Magnetic field of the nearby active M dwarf GJ 729, and a search for companions
summary: M dwarfs are prime targets for discovering exoplanets, and the nearest M dwarfs to the Sun provide among the best opportunities for follow-up detailed exoplanet characterization. GJ 729, the seventh closest M dwarf to the Sun, presents significant challenges for exoplanet detection due to its high levels of magnetic activity. To address this, we present a detailed analysis of GJ 729's magnetic field and its variability, followed by a search for exoplanets beneath the activity-induced noise in the stellar radial velocity. The geometry of GJ 729's large-scale magnetic field was reconstructed using new and archival spectropolarimetric data for a total of four epochs spanning 10 years. Results indicate a weak large-scale field ranging from 50 to 145 G, and an evolving non-axisymmetric field geometry that varies from poloidal dominated to a near-equal poloidal-toroidal configuration. We modeled activity-induced radial velocity variations using Gaussian Process Regression and activity diagnostics, and searched for planetary companions using ~90 d of high-cadence spectra taken contemporaneously with the high-precision CARMENES and HARPS spectrographs. Activity-only and activity + Keplerian models offered statistically equivalent fits, with a consistently preferred Keplerian period of ~7 d and amplitude of ~1.9 m/s across a range of activity modeling approaches. This could relate to an Earth-mass or Super-Earth planet, or residual stellar activity with power concentrated at a multiple of the rotation half-period. Our findings provide insight into the magnetic behavior of fully convective M dwarfs, and highlight the potential and challenges of detecting Keplerian RV signatures that are only a fraction of activity amplitudes.

AI.tldr: Study of GJ 729 (7th closest M dwarf to Sun) reconstructs its magnetic field across 10 years, finding weak (50-145 G) evolving fields. Despite high activity noise, a candidate ~7-day, ~1.9 m/s Keplerian signal is identified that could be an Earth-mass/Super-Earth planet or residual stellar activity at a multiple of the rotation half-period.
AI.motivation: M dwarfs are prime exoplanet targets, but GJ 729's high magnetic activity creates significant challenges for exoplanet detection via radial velocity. Understanding and mitigating this activity noise is necessary to search for planets beneath it.
AI.method: Large-scale magnetic field geometry reconstructed using new and archival spectropolarimetric data across four epochs spanning 10 years. Activity-induced RV variations modeled using Gaussian Process Regression with activity diagnostics. Planetary search using ~90 days of high-cadence CARMENES and HARPS spectra comparing activity-only vs. activity+Keplerian models.
AI.result: Weak large-scale field (50-145 G) with evolving non-axisymmetric geometry transitioning from poloidal-dominated to near-equal poloidal-toroidal. Activity+Keplerian and activity-only models statistically equivalent, but a Keplerian period of ~7 days with ~1.9 m/s amplitude is consistently preferred.
AI.conclusion: The ~7-day signal could be an Earth-mass/Super-Earth planet or residual stellar activity at a multiple of the rotation half-period. Provides insight into magnetic behavior of fully convective M dwarfs and highlights challenges of detecting Keplerian RV signals that are only a fraction of activity amplitudes.

title: There is no single density: star-forming regions and galaxies hold more dense ionized gas than long assumed
summary: Ionized gas fills star-forming regions and galaxies, and nearly everything we know about its temperature, pressure, mass, and composition is inferred from its emission lines [1-3]. The electron density is needed for all of these, yet a longstanding puzzle has resisted explanation: different density-sensitive lines, applied to the same gas, return values that disagree by up to two orders of magnitude. This is usually attributed either to each line tracing a physically distinct ionization zone or to imperfect atomic data [4-7]. Here we show that the disagreement is neither a flaw in the atomic data nor an ionization-stratification effect, but something more fundamental. Each diagnostic is tuned to a particular density, and when a nebula contains gas across a wide range of densities, as real nebulae do, each line reports the part of that range it is most sensitive to. The diagnostics do not measure a representative average density; they respond to different parts of a broad density distribution. This resolves the discrepancy with a simple relation between the density each line returns and the density it is most sensitive to, a relation that holds from individual H II regions to whole galaxies, near and far, and reveals that ionized nebulae contain far more dense gas than any one diagnostic implies. A nebula has no single electron density to measure, but a broad density distribution, and the masses, pressures, abundances and energetics built on the single-density assumption must be reconsidered, from nearby star-forming regions to galaxies across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves a long-standing puzzle where different density-sensitive emission lines in ionized gas (nebulae, H II regions, galaxies) disagree by up to two orders of magnitude. It shows this is not due to atomic data errors or ionization stratification, but because each diagnostic is tuned to a specific density in a broad density distribution. Real nebulae contain gas across a wide range of densities, and each line reports only the part it is most sensitive to, not a representative average. This reveals that nebulae have no single electron density but a broad distribution, requiring a reconsideration of derived masses, pressures, abundances, and energetics.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing discrepancy of up to two orders of magnitude between different density-sensitive emission line diagnostics applied to the same ionized gas, which has been puzzling astrophysicists despite being attributed to ionization stratification or imperfect atomic data.
AI.method: The paper demonstrates that each density-sensitive diagnostic is tuned to a particular density; when a nebula contains gas across a wide range of densities, each line reports the part of that range it is most sensitive to, rather than a representative average. A simple relation is derived between the density each line returns and the density it is most sensitive to, validated from individual H II regions to whole galaxies.
AI.result: The disagreement is not a flaw in atomic data nor an ionization-stratification effect but a fundamental issue: different diagnostics respond to different parts of a broad density distribution. Ionized nebulae contain far more dense gas than any single diagnostic implies, and no single electron density exists for a nebula.
AI.conclusion: The single-density assumption underlying derived masses, pressures, abundances, and energetics must be reconsidered, affecting interpretations from nearby star-forming regions to galaxies across cosmic time.

title: CARPP: Parametric Radiative-Transfer Fitting of Molecular Cores from Dust Continuum Data
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: The density profiles of dense molecular cores are important indicators of their physical and evolutionary states. Multi-wavelength dust continuum data offers excellent constraints on the density profile of cores. Here we introduce CARPP (Core Analysis via Radiative Transfer and Profile Parameters), a publicly available fitting package that generates optimized core density and temperature profiles based on parameterized radiative transfer calculations. CARPP assumes spherical symmetry and adopts physically motivated parametric forms for the density and temperature profiles, and uses dust continuum data for fitting. Tests on synthetic data show that CARPP achieves high accuracy, namely averaged relative errors of CARPP's seven parameters being $<20\%$, when the data quality satisfies $\frac{\rm RMS \,\, noise}{[\rm peak \,\, flux]} < 0.025\times \frac{[r_0]}{\rm resolution} +0.05$, where $r_0$ is the core's characteristic radius. We select the low-mass core TMC-1C and the high-mass core Ori2-2 to demonstrate CARPP's performance on real data. It classifies TMC-1C as a Bonnor-Ebert sphere in near-hydrostatic equilibrium, while Ori2-2 exhibits a power-law-dominated profile indicative of a collapsing envelope. This capability establishes CARPP as a powerful and versatile tool to classify the dynamical states of individual cores. It offers an optimal balance between physical fidelity and computational efficiency, serving as a practical, standardized alternative to both over-simplified SED analyses and complex, time-intensive 3D radiative-transfer modeling.

AI.tldr: CARPP is a publicly available fitting package that generates optimized density and temperature profiles of dense molecular cores using parameterized radiative transfer calculations and multi-wavelength dust continuum data, achieving high accuracy and serving as a practical tool for classifying core dynamical states.
AI.motivation: Density profiles of dense molecular cores are important indicators of their physical and evolutionary states, and multi-wavelength dust continuum data offers excellent constraints that require a standardized yet physically robust fitting tool.
AI.method: CARPP assumes spherical symmetry, adopts physically motivated parametric forms for density and temperature profiles, performs parameterized radiative transfer calculations, and fits dust continuum data. It includes a data quality criterion (RMS noise/peak flux < 0.025 × (r₀/resolution) + 0.05) for reliable parameter recovery.
AI.result: Tests on synthetic data show averaged relative errors of CARPP's seven parameters below 20% under the specified data quality condition. On real data, CARPP classified TMC-1C as a Bonnor-Ebert sphere in near-hydrostatic equilibrium and Ori2-2 as a power-law-dominated collapsing envelope.
AI.conclusion: CARPP is a powerful and versatile tool for classifying the dynamical states of individual cores, offering an optimal balance between physical fidelity and computational efficiency, serving as a practical alternative to both over-simplified SED analyses and complex 3D radiative-transfer modeling.

title: Beryllium enhancement in stars of the accreted Thamnos-2 system
summary: Surveys of Galactic halo stars have revealed numerous streams and substructures tracing stellar populations accreted by the Milky Way. Among these, Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) and Sequoia are the most prominent, both associated with dwarf galaxies accreted about 10 Gyr ago. We aim to measure beryllium abundances in nine stars associated with Thamnos, a substructure possibly linked to Sequoia, following the discovery of a Be-rich star BPM3066 by Monaco et al (2025). We used Gaia photometry and parallaxes to compute ATLAS9 model atmospheres. Synthetic spectra were generated with Turbospectrum and used with MyGIsFOS in single-model mode to analyze UVES high resolution spectra. Four new stars exhibit a significant beryllium overabundance. Moreover, the two known Be-rich stars, HD 106038 and HD 132475, are also found consistent with Thamnos membership. Thus, all currently known Be-rich stars appear associated with the Thamnos-2 structure. The Be enhancement is accompanied by elevated Si abundances, and we detect a correlation between Be and neutron-capture elements. No comparable Be-rich population is known elsewhere in the Galaxy, pointing to a rare enrichment event. The measured A(Be)/A(Li) excess ratio bears the imprint of spallation reactions, pointing to a highly energetic event in which fast CNO nuclei fragmented upon collision with the surrounding medium. The silicon overabundance is also consistent with a hypernova origin. Such an event may have rapidly enriched the surrounding gas to [Fe/H] about -1.5 explaining the relatively high metallicities of stars formed from this material despite their old ages (about 13 Gyr).

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that all known beryllium-rich stars in the Milky Way are associated with the Thamnos-2 substructure, and finds that their Be enhancement is correlated with elevated Si and neutron-capture elements, pointing to a rare hypernova-like spallation enrichment event about 13 Gyr ago.
AI.motivation: To investigate beryllium abundances in stars associated with the Thamnos substructure (possibly linked to Sequoia), following the discovery of a Be-rich star BPM3066, and to understand whether Be-rich stars are systematically linked to a specific accretion event.
AI.method: Gaia photometry and parallaxes were used to compute ATLAS9 model atmospheres. Synthetic spectra were generated with Turbospectrum and analyzed using MyGIsFOS in single-model mode on UVES high-resolution spectra. Beryllium abundances were measured in nine Thamnos-associated stars.
AI.result: Four new stars show significant Be overabundance. Two previously known Be-rich stars (HD 106038 and HD 132475) are also consistent with Thamnos membership. All known Be-rich stars are now associated with Thamnos-2. Be enhancement correlates with elevated Si and neutron-capture elements. The A(Be)/A(Li) ratio indicates spallation reactions, and Si overabundance is consistent with a hypernova origin.
AI.conclusion: A rare, highly energetic enrichment event (likely a hypernova) occurred about 13 Gyr ago, producing spallation-driven Be enhancement and enriching surrounding gas to [Fe/H] ~ -1.5, explaining the relatively high metallicities of these old stars. No comparable Be-rich population is known elsewhere in the Galaxy.

title: Subaru meets JWST: A Direct Measurement of Ly$\boldsymbolα$ Escape Fraction at $\boldsymbol{z\simeq6.2}$ with Dual Narrow-Band Imaging
summary: We present a direct measurement of the Ly$α$ escape fraction, $f^{\rm Lyα}_{\rm esc}$, for H$α$ emitters (HAEs) at $z\simeq6.2$ in the JWST CEERS field by combining JWST/NIRCam F470N imaging with Subaru/HSC NB872 imaging. This unique pair of narrow-band filters enables the simultaneous measurement of Ly$α$ and H$α$ fluxes from galaxies during the epoch of reionization (EoR). We select 84 HAEs from F470N excesses, among which 56 have reliable NB872 photometry and 19 are detected in Ly$α$ at $>2σ$ significance. The completeness-weighted stack of the HAE sample yields a median $f^{\rm Lyα}_{\rm esc}$ at $z\simeq6.2$ of $0.106^{+0.066}_{-0.044}$, which is in good agreement with recent measurements at similar redshifts. We further find no significant dependence of the stacked $f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Lyα}$ on the lower limit of H$α$ luminosity over the luminosity range probed by our sample. If Ly$α$ escape traces Lyman continuum leakage, this may suggest that relatively luminous HAEs, rather than only the faintest galaxies, can provide an important contribution to the ionizing photon budget during the EoR. For individual galaxies, $f^{\rm Lyα}_{\rm esc}$ positively correlates with Ly$α$ equivalent width and negatively correlates with the UV continuum slope $β$ and the rest-frame UV size, while no significant correlation is found with SED-derived $E(B-V)$, or rest-frame optical size, although these trends are based on a limited sample. These results suggest that the galaxy-to-galaxy variation in $f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Lyα}$ is more closely linked to compact, low-attenuation star-forming components traced by the UV continuum than to global dust attenuation or the overall stellar structure.

AI.tldr: This work measures the Lyα escape fraction at z≃6.2 for 84 HAEs using JWST/NIRCam F470N and Subaru/HSC NB872 imaging, finding a median f_esc^Lyα = 0.106^{+0.066}_{-0.044}, with no strong luminosity dependence, and correlations suggesting f_esc^Lyα is linked to compact, low-attenuation UV star-forming components rather than global dust or stellar structure.
AI.motivation: To directly measure the Lyα escape fraction for Hα emitters at z~6.2 during the epoch of reionization using a unique narrowband filter pair (JWST F470N and Subaru NB872) that simultaneously probes Lyα and Hα, in order to understand the role of galaxies in cosmic reionization and whether Lyα escape can serve as a proxy for Lyman continuum leakage.
AI.method: Select 84 HAEs from JWST/NIRCam F470N excess, cross-match with Subaru/HSC NB872 for Lyα; perform completeness-weighted stacking to derive median f_esc^Lyα; analyze correlations with Hα luminosity, Lyα EW, UV slope β, UV/optical sizes, and dust attenuation E(B-V).
AI.result: Median f_esc^Lyα = 0.106^{+0.066}_{-0.044} at z~6.2; no significant dependence on Hα luminosity lower limit; positive correlation with Lyα EW, negative correlations with UV slope β and rest-frame UV size; no significant correlation with E(B-V) or rest-frame optical size.
AI.conclusion: The measured f_esc^Lyα agrees with recent similar-redshift results; luminous HAEs may contribute importantly to the ionizing photon budget; galaxy-to-galaxy variation in f_esc^Lyα is driven by compact, low-attenuation star-forming regions rather than global dust or stellar structure.

title: Successive Coronal Jets as Novel Facilitators for Filament Oscillation and Eruption
summary: Solar filament eruptions are central to coronal mass ejections and space weather, yet their triggering mechanisms remain a fundamental open question. In particular, the early-stage that drives a magnetic flux rope toward instability and its observable signatures are poorly understood. Here, combining multi-instrument observations, we report successive coronal jets impacting a filament, causing its gradual rise and oscillations with growing amplitude and period. When the filament reaches the height where the decay index exceeds the torus instability threshold, the rapid filament eruption commences. This filament eruption is reproduced by magnetohydrodynamic simulations, in which successive thermal jets disturb a stable filament in a magnetic flux rope and excite oscillations together with the eruption of the filament. As the filament rises to erupt, the restoring forces for the oscillation progressively weaken, which naturally leads to an increase of the oscillation amplitude and period. Our results demonstrate the growing oscillations as one of the observable precursors for filament eruptions, enhancing our ability to predict solar eruptions.

AI.tldr: Combining observations and MHD simulations, we show that successive coronal jets impact a stable filament, causing it to rise and oscillate with growing amplitude and period until it reaches the torus instability threshold, triggering eruption. Growing oscillations serve as observable precursors for filament eruptions.
AI.motivation: Solar filament eruption triggering mechanisms remain poorly understood, especially the early-stage driving a magnetic flux rope toward instability and its observable signatures.
AI.method: Multi-instrument observations combined with magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of successive thermal jets disturbing a stable filament in a magnetic flux rope.
AI.result: Coronal jets cause gradual filament rise and oscillations with growing amplitude and period. Eruption commences when the filament reaches height where decay index exceeds the torus instability threshold. Oscillation amplitude/period increase naturally as restoring forces weaken during the rise.
AI.conclusion: Growing oscillations are observable precursors for filament eruptions, enhancing predictive capability for solar eruptions.

title: Collisionless and collisional kinetics of a plasma atmosphere with spatially and temporally intermittent heating at its base
summary: The solar corona exhibits a pronounced temperature inversion, with plasma temperatures increasing by nearly two orders of magnitude from the chromosphere to the corona. We investigate how spatially sparse and temporally intermittent stochastic heating at the base of the transition region shapes the temperature and density structure of coronal loops within a kinetic framework. Stochastic thermal boundary conditions and surface coarse graining are introduced. Analytical solutions are derived in the collisionless limit for heating-event time scales shorter or longer than the particle crossing time, and Coulomb collisions are incorporated through a reduced kinetic model describing the thermalization of suprathermal particles. In the short-time-scale regime, spatial filling factor and temporal intermittency combine into a single effective parameter controlling the suprathermal population, producing a transition region and a hot corona both within individual loops and after coarse graining. Collisions preserve this thermal structure while reducing the coronal density through progressive thermalization. In the long-time-scale regime, individual loops are nearly isothermal and the temperature inversion emerges only after coarse graining, depending solely on the spatial filling factor. Here, Coulomb collisions and optically thin radiative losses have only minor effects, while density and temperature profiles remain broadly consistent with coronal observations. These results show that sparse, intermittent heating naturally generates suprathermal particle distributions and reproduces the observed thermal structure of the solar corona within a kinetic framework, highlighting the different sensitivity of the two regimes to collisional effects.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how sparse, intermittent stochastic heating at the base of the transition region can explain the solar corona's temperature inversion (chromosphere to corona) using a kinetic framework. Two regimes are identified based on heating-event time scales relative to particle crossing times, each with distinct roles for collisions and coarse graining in producing coronal thermal structure.
AI.motivation: To understand how spatially sparse and temporally intermittent stochastic heating at the base of the transition region shapes the temperature and density structure of coronal loops, explaining the pronounced temperature inversion (two orders of magnitude) from the chromosphere to the corona.
AI.method: Kinetic framework with stochastic thermal boundary conditions and surface coarse graining; analytical solutions in the collisionless limit for two regimes (short vs. long heating-event time scales relative to particle crossing time); reduced kinetic model incorporating Coulomb collisions for suprathermal particle thermalization.
AI.result: Short-time-scale regime: spatial filling factor and temporal intermittency combine into a single effective parameter controlling the suprathermal population, producing a transition region and hot corona within individual loops and after coarse graining; collisions preserve thermal structure but reduce coronal density. Long-time-scale regime: individual loops are nearly isothermal, temperature inversion emerges only after coarse graining depending solely on spatial filling factor; collisions and radiative losses have minor effects; density/temperature profiles consistent with observations.
AI.conclusion: Sparse, intermittent heating naturally generates suprathermal particle distributions and reproduces the observed thermal structure of the solar corona within a kinetic framework, with the two regimes showing different sensitivity to collisional effects.

title: Long-term speckle interferometric monitoring of binary systems II: 2007-2025 positional measurements and improvement of orbits
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in the Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: This article is focused on the analysis of observational data and improvement of orbital solutions of 8 objects. The listed objects are members of a sample of approximately 300 nearby (d < 100 pc) multiple systems compiled for long-term monitoring at the 6-meter telescope of the Special Astrophysical Observatory of the Russian Academy of Sciences. Speckle interferometric observations were carried out from 2007 to the present, which corresponds to 19 years of monitoring of the systems. Therefore, the new measurements are more numerous than or comparable to those in the literature, which makes it possible to make the observation series more complete. A long observation series made it possible to cover from 20% to 70% of the phases of the orbital periods of the objects under study. In combination with previously published data, the percentage of orbital coverage by measurements ranged from 45% to 85%. As a result, 4 orbits were classified as "definitive", one as "good", 2 as "reliable", and one as "preliminary" according to a grading scheme suggested by W.I. Hartkopf et al. Despite the high grades of the orbital solutions, it is recommended to continue monitoring (in particular, to obtain periastron observations) for HIP 1055, HIP 2532, HIP 15633, HIP 19472 and HIP 20751 in order to derive the final orbital parameters. It is not possible to obtain an accurate orbital solution for HIP 20227 due to measurements whose assigned weight strongly influences the period value, and for HIP 21710(Aa,Ab) due to the long orbital period (Porb > 200 yr) and, consequently, the lack of observational data. An analysis and comparison of the mass sums and masses of components obtained by two independent methods and based on several parallax values were also carried out. In most cases, the best agreement is found between fundamental parameters calculated using Gaia parallaxes, if available.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes observational data and improves orbital solutions for 8 multiple star systems from a sample of ~300 nearby systems monitored for 19 years (2007–present) using speckle interferometry at the 6-meter telescope of SAO RAS. The new measurements increase orbital phase coverage to 45%–85% when combined with literature data. Four orbits are classified as "definitive," one as "good," two as "reliable," and one as "preliminary" per Hartkopf et al.'s grading scheme. Additional monitoring is recommended for five systems, while accurate solutions are not possible for two others due to measurement weighting issues and long orbital periods. Mass sums and component masses are compared using two independent methods and multiple parallax values, with best agreement found using Gaia parallaxes when available.
AI.motivation: To improve orbital solutions and characterize the dynamical properties of nearby multiple star systems through long-term speckle interferometric monitoring, using a 19-year observational baseline to achieve better orbital phase coverage and more accurate mass determinations.
AI.method: Speckle interferometric observations of 8 multiple systems from a sample of ~300 nearby (d < 100 pc) systems were conducted over 19 years (2007–present) using the 6-meter telescope of SAO RAS. New measurements were combined with published data to increase orbital phase coverage. Orbits were graded using Hartkopf et al.'s scheme. Mass sums and component masses were derived via two independent methods using multiple parallax values, including Gaia parallaxes.
AI.result: Orbital coverage from measurements ranged from 45% to 85% when combining new and literature data. Four orbits were graded "definitive," one "good," two "reliable," and one "preliminary." Mass sums and component masses showed best agreement when calculated using Gaia parallaxes. For HIP 20227, accurate orbit is precluded by weight-dependent period values; for HIP 21710(Aa,Ab), orbital period >200 yr prevents solution due to insufficient data.
AI.conclusion: Long-term speckle interferometric monitoring effectively improves orbital solutions for nearby multiple star systems, with most obtained orbits achieving high-grade classifications. Continued monitoring is recommended for five systems to obtain final orbital parameters, particularly periastron observations. Gaia parallaxes yield the most consistent mass determinations.

title: Effects of low resolution on the column density PDF of molecular clouds
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Observational resolution significantly impacts the interpretation of column density probability distribution functions (N-PDFs) in molecular clouds, which are essential for understanding turbulent structures and star formation processes. This study quantifies how low spatial resolution truncates the high-density power-law tails of N-PDFs by simulating distant observations (2-10 kpc) of 17 local massive molecular clouds/regions using Herschel-based column density maps. We propose a parameter-free model, assuming proportional embedding of dense regions within lower-density gas, to predict the truncation column density where the survival function equals the beam-to-threshold area ratio. Comparisons with simulations show good agreement, with deviations up to 0.3 dex attributed to cloud multiplicity in large complexes and flatter power-law tails in coherent structures. Characteristic cloud scales, derived from Delta-variance spectra, indicate that global smearing dominates when beam sizes exceed these scales. We further develop a reverse method to recover the intrinsic high-density tail from low-resolution data. Our findings link N-PDF shapes to morphologies, suggesting that feedback-compressed extended structures resist smearing, while multiplicity accelerates truncation. These insights caution against biases in N-PDF decompositions and provide a framework for correcting resolution effects in distant cloud studies, enhancing constraints on star formation theories.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies how low spatial resolution truncates high-density tails of column density PDFs in molecular clouds, proposes a parameter-free model to predict truncation, develops a reverse method to recover intrinsic tails, and links N-PDF shapes to cloud morphologies.
AI.motivation: Observational resolution significantly impacts the interpretation of N-PDFs in molecular clouds, which are essential for understanding turbulent structures and star formation processes. The study aims to quantify and correct for resolution-induced biases.
AI.method: Simulated distant observations (2-10 kpc) of 17 local massive clouds using Herschel-based column density maps; proposed a parameter-free model assuming proportional embedding of dense regions in lower-density gas; used Delta-variance spectra to derive characteristic cloud scales.
AI.result: Model predictions agree well with simulations (deviations up to 0.3 dex); global smearing dominates when beam sizes exceed characteristic cloud scales; feedback-compressed structures resist smearing while multiplicity accelerates truncation.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a framework for correcting resolution effects in distant cloud studies, caution against biases in N-PDF decompositions, and enhance constraints on star formation theories.

title: Multi-Path Quasi-Periodic Fast-mode Propagating Magnetoacoustic Waves to Diagnose Coronal Magnetic Field and Flaring Core
summary: Quasi-periodic fast-mode magnetoacoustic waves are often detected during solar flare events, although they are not observed in every flare, due to observational signal-to-noise limits and differences in flare magnetic topology and energy release strength. These structures propagate along magnetic configurations and supply effective diagnostics for coronal magnetic environments and flaring regions. Periodic signatures seen in fast-mode QFP wave trains carry physical information about excitation processes and propagation conditions. These signatures support quantitative studies of flare cores and magnetic channel properties. This work focuses on a well-documented event involving two oppositely oriented QFP waves simultaneously excited by a GOES-class M6.0 solar flare that occurred in active region NOAA 11261 on August 3, 2011. These QFP waves can be categorized into broad and narrow wave trains, with the narrow one propagating along funnel-like loops and the broad one moving through the low corona. Observational results suggest that both broad-wave and narrow-wave QFP phenomena can be simultaneously triggered by a single flare eruption. This study also indicates that such multi-path QFP wave events can be utilized to diagnose the magnetic field and the flare's core, and demonstrates the capability of multi-path QFP waves for robust coronal magnetic field and flare core diagnostics.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a dual-path QFP wave event (broad and narrow wave trains) simultaneously excited by an M6.0 solar flare on August 3, 2011, demonstrating their utility for diagnosing coronal magnetic fields and flare core properties.
AI.motivation: QFP waves are not always detected in flares due to signal-to-noise limits and variations in magnetic topology and energy release. This work aims to understand multi-path QFP wave excitation and leverage such events for robust diagnostics of coronal magnetic environments and flare cores.
AI.method: A well-documented M6.0 flare event (NOAA 11261, August 3, 2011) is studied, in which two oppositely oriented QFP wave trains (broad and narrow) were simultaneously triggered. The narrow wave propagates along funnel-like loops, while the broad wave moves through the low corona. Observational analysis categorizes and characterizes both wave trains.
AI.result: Both broad-wave and narrow-wave QFP phenomena can be simultaneously triggered by a single flare eruption. The multi-path QFP wave event provides measurable periodic signatures that encode information about excitation processes and propagation conditions.
AI.conclusion: Multi-path QFP wave events serve as effective tools for robust diagnostics of the coronal magnetic field and flare core structure, enabling quantitative studies of magnetic channel properties and flare energy release processes.

title: Constraints on the properties of warm ionized gas from low-frequency hydrogen radio recombination lines
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in AJ
summary: The ionized gas in the Milky Way is a major component of the interstellar medium. Observations of extinction free tracers, such as hydrogen radio recombination lines (HRRLs), have revealed the presence of a dense (electron density 1 to 100 cm$^{-3}$) warm ionized medium. Motivated by advances in radio instrumentation, the existence of fully sampled HRRL maps, and a better knowledge about the population of discrete HII regions in our Galaxy, we have acquired new low-frequency ($ν\lesssim1$ GHz) observations of HRRLs to characterize the properties of this gas. We target three positions in the Galactic plane, with few or no known HII regions, using the 342 MHz and 800 MHz feeds of the Green Bank Telescope. We detect HRRL emission from all three positions. We combine these with the fully sampled HRRL 5.8 GHz cubes from the GBT Diffuse Ionized Gas Survey (GDIGS) to determine the gas properties using a forward modeling approach. From our analysis we find electron densities between 6 and 15 cm$^{-3}$, and that to determine the gas temperature and emission measure we require informative priors or higher signal-to-noise observations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new low-frequency (≤1 GHz) hydrogen radio recombination line observations from the Green Bank Telescope at three positions in the Galactic plane with few known HII regions, detecting emission from all three. Combined with GDIGS 5.8 GHz data and forward modeling, the analysis yields electron densities of 6–15 cm⁻³, and shows that determining gas temperature and emission measure requires informative priors or higher signal-to-noise data.
AI.motivation: To characterize the properties of the dense warm ionized medium in the Milky Way using new low-frequency HRRL observations, motivated by advances in radio instrumentation, availability of fully sampled HRRL maps, and improved knowledge of discrete HII region populations.
AI.method: Acquired low-frequency (342 MHz and 800 MHz) HRRL observations using the Green Bank Telescope at three positions in the Galactic plane with few/no known HII regions. Combined these data with fully sampled HRRL 5.8 GHz cubes from the GBT Diffuse Ionized Gas Survey (GDIGS) and applied a forward modeling approach to determine gas properties.
AI.result: HRRL emission detected from all three positions. Electron densities found between 6 and 15 cm⁻³. Determining gas temperature and emission measure requires informative priors or higher signal-to-noise observations.
AI.conclusion: Low-frequency HRRL observations combined with higher-frequency GDIGS data and forward modeling can constrain electron densities of the warm ionized medium, but higher signal-to-noise or informative priors are needed for robust temperature and emission measure estimates.

title: Cataclysmic Variables Photometric Periods from TESS
summary: We present a sample of coherent and stable photometric period determinations for cataclysmic variables, based on TESS photometry through sector 102. We analyzed a total of 1557 cataclysmic variable stars and detected periodic variations in 1362 objects, including 286 eclipsing or ellipsoidal-variation systems, 63 polars, and 135 intermediate polars. In particular, we present the first determination of the optical variability period for 565 cataclysmic variables. Due to the 21x21" pixel size of TESS, we tested whether the variability was coming from the cataclysmic variable and not from a nearby star. For the intermediate polars, we detected spin periods in addition to orbital periods for 83 systems. We detect a clear period gap between ~2 and ~3 h in the eclipsing sample, consistent with previous work. The gap remains for the complete sample of photometric variability periods. There is no apparent gap in the orbital period distribution for intermediate polars. Finally, the median of the photometric period distribution of our complete sample of cataclysmic variables is 3.681 h. Comparing this to the distribution of rotation periods for likely single white dwarfs, we find a similar range, with a median photometric period of 6.803~h.

AI.tldr: Using TESS data (through sector 102), we analyzed 1557 cataclysmic variables, detecting periodic variations in 1362 objects. We provide first optical variability periods for 565 CVs, identify spin periods in 83 intermediate polars, confirm the ~2-3 h period gap in eclipsing systems, find no gap for intermediate polars, and report a median photometric period of 3.681 h for the full CV sample vs. 6.803 h for single white dwarfs.
AI.motivation: To systematically determine coherent, stable photometric periods for a large sample of cataclysmic variables using high-cadence TESS data, addressing the lack of period measurements for many known CVs and clarifying period distributions.
AI.method: Analysis of TESS photometry through sector 102 for 1557 cataclysmic variables; period detection via photometric variability; cross-check to ensure variability originates from the CV rather than nearby stars (given 21×21" pixel size); classification of eclipsing/ellipsoidal systems, polars, and intermediate polars; separation of spin and orbital periods in IPs.
AI.result: Periodic variations detected in 1362/1557 CVs, including 286 eclipsing/ellipsoidal, 63 polars, 135 IPs; first optical periods for 565 CVs; spin+orbital periods for 83 IPs; period gap confirmed at ~2-3 h in eclipsing sample; no gap in IP orbital periods; median period 3.681 h for full CV sample vs. 6.803 h for single white dwarfs.
AI.conclusion: TESS enables robust period determination for a large, homogeneous CV sample. The classical period gap persists in eclipsing systems, but IPs show no gap. The CV period distribution differs notably from that of single white dwarfs, with CVs having shorter median periods.

title: Disentangling the dark and stellar mass through precise lens modelling of the JWST observation of lensed quasar WFI2033--4723
summary: We use high-resolution JWST/NIRCam imaging and measured time delays to model the quadruply imaged quasar WFI2033--4723 with a composite stellar plus dark-matter mass model. We first construct an elliptical power-law baseline model and recover Fermat-potential differences (fpd) consistent with previous HST-based and JWST-based analyses, providing a reference scale for composite modelling. We then replace the total mass profile with a physically motivated decomposition in which the stellar mass follows a multi-Gaussian expansion of the lens light, with a free radial mass-to-light gradient, and the dark matter is described by a generalized Navarro--Frenk--White (gNFW) halo. Using two external cosmological priors, Planck+DESI and Pantheon+SH0ES, the measured time delays constrain the mass-sheet-transformation freedom that would otherwise damage the stellar--dark-matter decomposition. In both cosmological cases, the stellar normalization lies between the expectations for Chabrier and Salpeter initial mass functions, while the radial mass-to-light gradient is not strongly required by the data (mildly positive). The dark matter halo has an inner slope $γ_{\rm in}\simeq1.3$, steeper than a standard NFW cusp, and the main astrophysical conclusions are insensitive to the adopted cosmological prior. This work shows that composite time-delay lens modelling can effectively separate baryons from dark matter. As a qualitative check, we reverse the logic and use our composite lens model without kinematic information to infer the cosmology instead. However, the strong degeneracy between $H_0$ and the halo scale radius $R_s$ prevents a robust standalone constraint.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRCam imaging and time delays, the paper models the quadruply imaged quasar WFI2033–4723 with a composite stellar+dark-matter mass model. A baseline elliptical power-law model recovers consistent Fermat-potential differences. Replacing the total mass profile with a stellar (multi-Gaussian expansion with free radial mass-to-light gradient) plus gNFW dark-matter decomposition, and applying Planck+DESI or Pantheon+SH0ES priors, constrains the mass-sheet transformation. Stellar normalization lies between Chabrier and Salpeter IMFs; dark-matter inner slope is ~1.3 (steeper than NFW). Using the composite model without kinematics to infer cosmology is hampered by H0–Rs degeneracy.
AI.motivation: To separate baryonic and dark-matter components in strong gravitational lensing by combining high-resolution JWST imaging with measured time delays, overcoming the mass-sheet degeneracy via external cosmological priors.
AI.method: Composite lens modelling with stellar mass described by a multi-Gaussian expansion of the lens light (free radial mass-to-light gradient) and dark matter as a gNFW halo. Two external cosmological priors (Planck+DESI and Pantheon+SH0ES) constrain the mass-sheet-transformation freedom. Baseline elliptical power-law model provides reference Fermat-potential differences.

Dark-matter inner slope γ_in ≈ 1.3, steeper than standard NFW cusp. Main results are insensitive to the choice of cosmological prior. AI.conclusion: Composite time-delay lens modelling can effectively separate baryons from dark matter. However, using the composite model without kinematics yields a degenerate H0 constraint, confirming the need for additional information (e.g., stellar kinematics) to break degeneracies.
